Q: What do you remember about growing up in Salford?

A: It was rough, I won't pretend otherwise. Back-to-back houses, outside toilet, the whole lot. But everyone was the same so you didn't think anything of it. The street was your world when you were a kid — you were out from morning till dark and nobody worried. My mam would just open the door and shout and you came in. That was it.

Q: What was your father like?

A: He worked at the docks. Big man, very physical. Not what you'd call a talker. He'd come home, eat, sit by the fire, that was his evening. He wasn't unkind, he just — he didn't really know what to do with children, I think. His own father had been the same. It was just how men were then. You got on with things.

Q: How did National Service affect you?

A: More than I admitted at the time. You go in as a boy, really. I was eighteen. First time I'd been out of Salford, practically. They sent me to Cyprus — this was during the troubles there, EOKA and all that. Nothing I'd call proper combat, but it wasn't nothing either. You saw things. Came home and never really talked about it. My wife knew not to ask, after a while.

Q: How did you meet your wife, Jean?

A: At a works dance. Very glamorous. [dry laugh] She was there with another fella and I cut in and she let me, which I took as a good sign. She was from Stretford — her dad was not best pleased she was seeing someone from Salford, like I was from another country. We were married in 1961 and that was that. Fifty-two years. She went first, which I was glad of, in a way. She wouldn't have managed without me. I can manage without her. I just don't enjoy it much.

Q: What's the thing you're most proud of?

A: [pause] My kids all turned out decent. That's it, really. I wasn't the most patient father — I was at work a lot, and when I was home I was tired. I probably should have been around more. But they're all good people and they talk to me, which I think means I didn't do too badly. That's all you want, isn't it. That they still want to talk to you.
